title: Inside the Consultant Conversation: A Q&A with Holly Goodrich and Stephanie Lane
summary: Holly Goodrich, Global Head of Consultant & OCIO Relations, and Stephanie Lane, Consultant & OCIO Relations Strategy, discuss how consultants and OCIOs are rethinking portfolio construction, expanding into new client segments and building partnerships focused on long-term client outcomes.
body_markdown:
For fixed income and LDI portfolios, consultants are evaluating[p rivate investment-grade credit](https://www.apollo.com/strategies/asset-management/credit/investment-grade-private-credit) , including appropriate asset-backed finance exposures, against the same objectives that guide other investments: credit quality, duration, cash flows and liquidity needs. The question has become less about whether an investment is public or private and more about the role it can play in the portfolio.


As private assets become more integrated into broader portfolios, access to consistent pricing, reliable data and greater transparency becomes increasingly important. To help address this need, Apollo is[e xpanding daily pricing across its credit business](https://ir.apollo.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/654/apollo-expands-daily-pricing-to-all-credit-assets) , and we are an anchor partner in[ICE Private Credit Intelligence](https://ir.apollo.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/613/intercontinental-exchange-launches-ice-private-credit) , which is designed to support standardized data and greater transparency.


### Defined contribution is another area attracting significant attention. How do you see the role of private markets and retirement income evolving within DC and what does this mean for consultants?


**Holly Goodrich:** The starting point is retirement outcomes: helping participants build sufficient savings and turn those savings into income that can last throughout retirement. Consultants have an important role in helping plan sponsors evaluate a broader set of tools to meet those goals.


There is growing interest in bringing capabilities that have historically been available to defined benefit (DB) plans into DC. That includes access to private assets through professionally managed investment solutions, such as target date funds, as well as access to retirement income solutions. This gives plan sponsors more options to address participants’ long-term needs.


These are related but distinct needs. Private assets may provide additional sources of return and diversification, while insurance-based lifetime income solutions can help participants address the risk of outliving their savings. Our experience across asset management and retirement services through Athene reinforces the importance of considering investment strategies and retirement income solutions together.


Addressing these needs creates opportunities for collaboration among consultants, asset managers, insurers and plan sponsors, including those serving pooled employer plans and master trusts. Consultants can help navigate the distinct requirements of each market and plan structure. **


Bringing private assets into DC is not simply a matter of repackaging institutional strategies. Consultants are rightly focused on fiduciary considerations, valuation, liquidity, fees, operational integration and participant outcomes. Education and thoughtful product design are essential. Similarly, lifetime income solutions need to be understandable, accessible and integrated into the participant experience. The goal is not to add complexity, but to make these capabilities work more effectively for retirement savers.


### Consultants are looking to expand their presence in insurance and wealth management. What is driving this interest, and what opportunities does it present?


**Stephanie Lane:** Firms looking to extend their expertise beyond traditional pension plans are turning to insurance and wealth management as adjacent markets for their consulting and OCIO capabilities. Both allow firms to apply their portfolio construction, manager research and implementation expertise to a new set of clients.


Each market, however, has distinct needs. For insurers, the starting point is the liability. Investment decisions need to reflect liability profiles, regulatory capital requirements, liquidity needs and asset-liability matching. Through our work sourcing high-grade assets and managing insurance portfolios, we see firsthand the importance of these considerations as consultants expand their work with insurance clients.


In wealth management, the opportunity is to help advisors bring institutional-quality investment capabilities into portfolios in ways that are appropriate for their clients. That requires more than access to products. It includes portfolio construction support, appropriate investment structures, transparent reporting and ongoing education, with close attention to suitability, liquidity and fees.


As consulting firms build their presence in these markets, they are developing capabilities, partnerships and implementation models tailored to different client segments. Whether through investment advisory mandates, manager selection or OCIO relationships, consultants are applying investment expertise to meet the needs of the end investor.


### We are seeing consultants focus on building deeper strategic partnerships with asset managers. What is behind this shift, and how do you see these relationships evolving?


**Holly Goodrich:** Manager research and investment performance remain fundamental, while the breadth of the relationship with asset managers is expanding. As consultants grow their OCIO businesses into areas such as wealth and insurance, many are looking for strategic partners that can contribute across portfolio construction, implementation and the development of long-term solutions.
